claims.text: Overall wear resistance during high-temperature sliding is governed by coating grain size and the resulting grain-boundary density.
Microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding is governed by coating grain size and the resulting grain-boundary density.
Grain-boundary density influences diffusion-mediated creep deformation.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has an average grain size of 10 μm.
A controlled change in deposition parameters can reduce the coating's average grain size from 10 μm to 1 μm.
Reducing grain size from 10 μm to 1 μm changes the grain-boundary density.
Diffusion-mediated creep is the operative microscopic deformation mechanism in the stated sliding regime.
Reducing the average grain size from 10 μm to 1 μm will decrease wear rate by 30% relative to the baseline.
Reducing the average grain size from 10 μm to 1 μm will decrease microscopic deformation by 25% relative to the baseline.
The predicted changes apply between 500°C and 700°C.
Composition, substrate material, and surface roughness may also influence wear resistance and microscopic deformation.
Failure of wear rate and microscopic deformation to decrease by at least 20% relative to the baseline is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
